subject: Medicine
title: STEMI Localization & Culprit Coronary Arteries
preview: Localize possible culprit coronary territories on the ECG without treating lead patterns as absolute arterial proof.

sections.title: ECG territory clues
points: V1–V4 can suggest anterior involvement; II, III and aVF suggest inferior involvement; I, aVL, V5–V6 may suggest lateral involvement.
Coronary dominance and anatomical variation mean an ECG territory does not uniquely identify the occluded artery.

sections.title: Assess right ventricular involvement
points: Inferior infarction with hypotension, clear lungs and raised jugular venous pressure should prompt right-sided ECG assessment and urgent specialist management.
Avoid therapies that could worsen hemodynamic instability; evaluate volume and right-heart physiology rather than using automatic aggressive fluid boluses.

sections.title: Exam trap
points: A normal or nondiagnostic initial ECG does not fully exclude acute coronary syndrome.
Do not apply a single rigid medication rule without the patient’s blood pressure and clinical context.

quickRevision: Anterior ST elevation often implicates LAD territory; inferior ST elevation may reflect RCA or circumflex involvement.
Posterior infarction may produce reciprocal anterior ST depression; posterior leads can improve detection.
Right ventricular involvement changes hemodynamic management and requires careful assessment.

quiz.question: ST elevation in inferior leads II, III and aVF suggests injury in which wall?
options: Posterior wall as the only site
quiz.explanation: Inferior wall. V1–V4 can suggest anterior involvement; II, III and aVF suggest inferior involvement; I, aVL, V5–V6 may suggest lateral involvement.
